procedures.title: Mass Casualty Triage — START / SALT Execution
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Mass Casualty
procedures.subtitle: The initial sort when casualties outstrip resources. Two frameworks, one discipline: sort fast, intervene minimally, keep moving, reassess constantly.
procedures.description: The initial sort when casualties outstrip resources.

blocks.html:
• Any incident where the number of casualties exceeds immediately available resources (mass casualty incident, MCI)
  • Applies at the scene during the initial sorting pass, before individualized patient care begins
  • START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) is the most widely used initial sort in the US prehospital system; SALT (Sort, Assess, Lifesaving interventions, Treatment/transport) is the current national model integrating a global sort step and limited lifesaving interventions
• None — the framework applies whenever resources are outstripped by casualty volume; the judgment call is whether an MCI declaration is warranted, not whether to triage once declared

• Triage tags/tape (color-coded: Red/Immediate, Yellow/Delayed, Green/Minor, Black/Expectant or deceased)
  • Simple airway adjuncts for lifesaving interventions only (oral airway, occlusive dressing for open chest wound, tourniquet)
  • No diagnostic equipment, no IV starts, no detailed exams during the initial sort — this is a rapid pass, not treatment
START

steps.html: Direct all ambulatory patients to a designated area and tag them Green (Minor) — this immediately reduces the pool requiring individual assessment.

For each remaining patient, assess Respirations first: not breathing → open airway; still not breathing → Black (Expectant/Deceased). Breathing after repositioning, or RR >30/min → Red (Immediate). RR <30/min → proceed to perfusion.
Assess Perfusion (radial pulse present/absent, or cap refill): absent (or >2 sec) → control major hemorrhage if present, tag Red (Immediate). Present → proceed to mental status.
Assess Mental status (only if respirations and perfusion are within limits): unable to follow simple commands → Red (Immediate). Able to follow commands → Yellow (Delayed).
Move to the next patient — the entire assessment should take under 60 seconds per patient.

blocks.html: SALT

steps.html: Sort: Global voice sort — call out for anyone who can walk to move to one area (assess last), then anyone who can wave or purposefully move to another area (assess second), leaving non-purposeful movers/obviously injured to be assessed first.
Assess each patient in that priority order (still, then waving, then walking), applying lifesaving interventions as you go rather than deferring.

Lifesaving interventions performed during assessment, not withheld: open airway, control major hemorrhage (tourniquet/wound packing), chest decompression for tension physiology, auto-injector antidotes if indicated (e.g., nerve agent exposure).

Assign triage category after interventions: obeys commands, has a pulse, no respiratory distress, hemorrhage controlled → likely to survive with current resources → Immediate or Delayed based on injury severity. Injuries incompatible with survival given available resources → Expectant. No signs of life after airway opened, no obvious reason for futility → Dead.
Reassess and re-triage as resources or patient status change — MCI triage is dynamic, not a single pass.

blocks.title: Global sort before individual assessment
blocks.html: The walk/wave/still voice sort does most of the categorization work before hands ever touch a patient — resist the pull to fully manage the first critical patient found at the expense of sorting the rest of the scene.

• Getting pulled into treating one patient at the expense of the global sort — the initial pass is deliberately superficial
  • Failing to reassess — Yellow/Delayed patients can deteriorate; triage is iterative through the incident
  • Over-triage saturating resources — tagging too many patients Red degrades the ability to treat the truly immediate
  • Under-triage from anchoring on scene chaos — a quiet, still patient may be worse off than a loud one
  • Confusing the triage officer role with the treatment role — the job is to sort and move, not provide ongoing care to any single patient

The global voice sort in SALT (walk/wave/still) does most of the categorization work before you ever lay hands on a patient.

Lifesaving interventions during SALT are deliberately limited to airway, hemorrhage, decompression, and antidotes — anything beyond belongs in the treatment phase.

Speak your tag category out loud as you assign it — this creates a running verbal count for incident command and catches your own errors in real time.

Whichever system your agency/region has adopted, the discipline is identical: sort fast, intervene minimally, keep moving.

procedures.title: Arterial Line Placement During Resuscitation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Vascular Access / Circulatory
procedures.subtitle: Real-time hemodynamic monitoring when non-invasive measurement isn't keeping up with how fast the patient is changing.
procedures.description: Real-time hemodynamics when non-invasive monitoring lags.

blocks.html:
• Need for continuous, beat-to-beat blood pressure monitoring during active resuscitation or hemodynamic instability
  • Frequent arterial blood gas sampling anticipated
  • Titration of vasopressors/inotropes where non-invasive cuff measurements are too slow or unreliable (e.g., low-flow states)

• Inadequate collateral circulation at the intended site (e.g., abnormal Allen's test for radial site, though rarely a hard stop in an emergency)
  • Local infection or significant trauma overlying the intended site
  • Severe peripheral vascular disease at the intended site (relative — choose an alternate site)

• Arterial line catheter kit (typically 20 ga for radial, larger for femoral)
  • Ultrasound with linear probe (recommended, especially in low-flow/hypotensive states)
  • Pressure transducer, tubing, pressure bag with flush solution
  • Local anesthetic if patient is responsive

steps.html: Select the site — radial artery is typical first choice for accessibility and complication profile; femoral artery for faster access in profound shock or when radial pulses are difficult to palpate.
Position the extremity appropriately (wrist extension for radial access).
Prep the site; use ultrasound guidance if available, especially with weak or absent palpable pulses.
Insert the catheter-over-needle or catheter-over-wire (Seldinger) system at a shallow angle, advancing until arterial flash is seen.
Advance the catheter into the vessel, confirm pulsatile return.
Connect to the pressure tubing/transducer system, zero and level the transducer.
Secure the catheter, confirm waveform quality on the monitor.

blocks.title: Palpable pulses can be absent even when a line is achievable
blocks.html: In profound shock, ultrasound guidance becomes far more valuable in exactly the situations where the line is most urgently needed — don't let a difficult radial site delay you from moving to femoral access.

• Thrombosis or distal ischemia — monitor the extremity distal to the line regularly
  • Hematoma or bleeding at the site, especially with coagulopathy
  • Infection with prolonged dwell time
  • Inadvertent intra-arterial medication injection if the line is mistaken for venous access — label clearly
  • Damped or inaccurate waveform from catheter kinking, air in the system, or poor positioning

In profound shock, palpable pulses may be absent even with adequate arterial pressure for a line — ultrasound guidance becomes far more valuable in exactly the situations where you need the line most urgently.

Femoral access is often faster and more reliable than radial in a critically hypotensive patient — don't force a technically harder site when time and accuracy both matter.

Zero and level the transducer at the phlebostatic axis for femoral or central-adjacent sites to avoid a systematically inaccurate reading.

procedures.title: Central Line Placement Under Arrest Conditions
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Vascular Access / Circulatory
procedures.subtitle: Femoral-first access during active resuscitation — landmark or ultrasound-guided, without interrupting compressions.
procedures.description: Femoral-first access without interrupting compressions.

blocks.html:
• Need for reliable central access during cardiac arrest or peri-arrest resuscitation when IO/peripheral access is inadequate or unavailable
  • High-dose vasopressor administration, rapid volume resuscitation, or need for central venous monitoring during ongoing resuscitation
  • Anticipated prolonged resuscitation (e.g., ECPR candidacy) where central access will be needed regardless

• Active CPR at the intended site preventing safe access (femoral line placement should not interrupt or interfere with ongoing compressions — choose a site and technique that coexists with compressions)
  • Known femoral vascular injury or prior femoral graft at the intended site (relative — choose alternate side or site)
  • Coagulopathy is a relative, not absolute, contraindication in the arrest setting given the urgency of the indication

• Central line kit (triple-lumen or appropriate for indication)
  • Ultrasound with linear probe if available and time allows
  • Chlorhexidine prep, sterile technique as feasible given the emergent context
  • Guidewire, dilator, catheter per Seldinger technique

steps.html: Choose the femoral vein as the default site during active arrest — it does not require interrupting compressions or airway management, unlike subclavian or internal jugular approaches.
Identify landmarks: femoral vein lies medial to the femoral artery, below the inguinal ligament (use ultrasound if immediately available without delaying access).
Insert the needle at a 30-45 degree angle, aspirating as you advance, aiming just medial to the palpated or visualized arterial pulse.
Confirm venous return (dark, non-pulsatile blood), thread the guidewire.
Make a small skin nick, dilate the tract.
Advance the catheter over the wire to the appropriate depth, remove the wire.
Aspirate and flush all ports, secure the catheter.
Obtain confirmatory imaging or clinical confirmation once the immediate resuscitation allows; reassess placement once the code concludes.

blocks.title: Femoral is the default during active compressions
blocks.html: It's the one site that doesn't compete with the airway or the person doing chest compressions — don't let the pursuit of ultrasound guidance delay access if landmark technique is faster and the operator is confident.

• Arterial puncture — apply direct pressure, do not remove the needle blindly if committed to the wire without confirming venous placement first
  • Guidewire embolization if not held securely at all times
  • Infection risk elevated given compromised sterile technique in an emergent setting — plan for line exchange once the patient is stabilized
  • Delayed recognition of arterial cannulation if committed to dilation before confirming venous return

Femoral access is the default during active compressions because it's the one site that doesn't compete with the airway or the person doing compressions.

Don't let the pursuit of ultrasound guidance delay access if landmark technique is faster and the operator is confident — use whichever gets you reliable access soonest.

Any line placed under emergent, imperfect sterile conditions should be flagged for exchange once the patient is stabilized.

procedures.title: ECMO Cannulation Prep & Activation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Vascular Access / Circulatory
procedures.subtitle: Peripheral VA/VV cannulation framework, from activation call to first flow — and the timing discipline that drives ECPR outcomes more than technique does.
procedures.description: VA/VV framework from activation call to first flow.

blocks.html:
VA-ECMO

  • Refractory cardiogenic shock
  • ECPR for witnessed arrest with high-quality CPR and a reversible/treatable cause
  • Post-cardiotomy shock
  • Massive PE with hemodynamic collapse
  • Severe hypothermia with cardiac instability (rewarming crossover)

VV-ECMO

  • Severe refractory hypoxemic and/or hypercapnic respiratory failure despite optimized mechanical ventilation and adjuncts (proning, paralysis, inhaled pulmonary vasodilators)

General

  • Bridge to recovery, bridge to durable device/transplant, or bridge to decision

• Unwitnessed arrest or prolonged downtime with no ROSC and poor CPR quality (for ECPR specifically)
  • Irreversible/non-survivable underlying condition
  • Severe pre-existing multi-organ failure incompatible with meaningful recovery
  • Uncontrolled hemorrhage (relative — requires concurrent source control planning)
  • Lack of institutional capability to manage ECMO post-cannulation (relative to transfer feasibility)

• ECMO cannulation kit (arterial and venous cannulae, sized per patient)
  • Ultrasound (vascular access, cannula tip confirmation)
  • Guidewires, dilators, introducer sheaths
  • Circuit primed and de-aired (pump, oxygenator, tubing) per institutional protocol
  • Anticoagulation (heparin) and ACT monitoring capability
  • Fluoroscopy or TEE if available for cannula positioning confirmation
  • Full cannulation team: proceduralist, circuit specialist/perfusion, nursing, airway/code team continuing resuscitation in parallel for ECPR
Peripheral VA cannulation &mdash; general framework

steps.html: Activate ECMO team early — call the moment criteria are anticipated, not once decompensation is complete.
Continue resuscitation (compressions, ventilation, vasopressors) uninterrupted during setup for ECPR cases.
Prime and de-air circuit in parallel with access — do not let circuit prep be the bottleneck.
Obtain venous access (typically femoral vein) via ultrasound-guided Seldinger technique; serially dilate to accommodate venous cannula.
Obtain arterial access (typically femoral artery) via ultrasound-guided Seldinger technique; consider a distal perfusion catheter to mitigate limb ischemia.
Advance venous cannula to the cavoatrial junction; advance arterial cannula per sizing/institutional target.
Confirm cannula position (fluoroscopy, TEE, or venous blood gas from the venous limb as a surrogate) before connecting to circuit.
Connect cannulae to primed circuit, eliminating air at every connection.
Initiate flow at low RPM, titrate up while monitoring hemodynamics, oxygenation, and circuit pressures.
Anticoagulate per protocol once bleeding risk is assessed; establish ACT/anti-Xa monitoring.
Secure cannulae, obtain confirmatory imaging (CXR, or fluoroscopy if not already done), and transition to ICU-level ECMO management.

blocks.title: Activation delay is the single biggest modifiable factor
blocks.html: For ECPR specifically, time from arrest to flow drives outcome more than any technical detail of the cannulation itself — call for activation the moment ECMO becomes a real possibility, not once every other option has failed.

• Limb ischemia distal to arterial cannula — have a distal perfusion catheter plan ready, not as an afterthought
  • Air embolism during cannulation or connection — de-air meticulously at every step
  • Malposition (venous cannula against a wall, arterial cannula too proximal/distal) — confirm before committing flow
  • Bleeding at access sites, worsened once anticoagulated
  • Delayed activation — the single biggest modifiable factor in ECPR outcomes is time from arrest to flow
  • Harlequin syndrome (differential hypoxia) in peripheral VA-ECMO with native cardiac recovery and poor lung function — may require venous cannula repositioning or conversion to VAV

The clock starts at low-flow/no-flow time, not at the decision to cannulate — activate the team the moment ECMO is a real possibility.

Two operators working access sites simultaneously (one venous, one arterial) meaningfully shortens time to flow.

Circuit priming is often the rate-limiting step, not the cannulation itself — get perfusion/circuit specialist moving in parallel from minute one.

Have your distal perfusion strategy decided before you need it, not while a limb is turning white on the table.

procedures.title: Intraosseous Access
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Vascular Access / Circulatory
procedures.subtitle: Proximal humerus, sternal, and tibial sites — the fastest reliable vascular access when peripheral IV attempts have failed or time doesn't allow for them.
procedures.description: Proximal humerus, sternal, and tibial sites.

blocks.html:
• Emergent need for vascular access when peripheral IV access is difficult, delayed, or has failed
  • Cardiac arrest (any age)
  • Hemorrhagic or other shock states requiring immediate fluid/medication access
  • Any critically ill or injured patient where seconds of delay matter

• Fracture at or proximal to the intended insertion site
  • Previous IO attempt or orthopedic hardware at the same site within the prior 24-48 hours
  • Infection (cellulitis) overlying the insertion site
  • Inability to identify landmarks confidently (relative — choose an alternate site)

• IO driver (manual or powered, e.g., spring-loaded or drill-based device)
  • IO needle appropriate to site and patient size
  • Chlorhexidine or available skin prep
  • Extension tubing, syringe for aspiration/flush
  • Lidocaine for conscious patients (both at the skin and injected into the marrow space before infusion)
Proximal humerus

steps.html: Position the arm adducted, internally rotated, with the hand resting on the abdomen (this exposes the greater tubercle landmark).
Palpate the surgical neck of the humerus, approximately 1-2 cm above it for the insertion point.
Insert the IO needle perpendicular to the bone surface, driving through the cortex until a give/pop is felt.
Remove the stylet, confirm placement (needle stands firmly without support, marrow aspirate if attempted, free flow of flush without extravasation).
Secure and connect to extension tubing.

blocks.html: Sternal

steps.html: Identify the manubrium as the insertion site (device-specific — sternal IO devices use a dedicated targeting mechanism).
Follow the specific device protocol for insertion depth and technique.
Confirm placement per device indicator and flush test.

blocks.html: Tibial

steps.html: Identify the anteromedial tibial surface, approximately 1-2 cm below and medial to the tibial tuberosity in adults (adjust per pediatric landmarks).
Insert perpendicular to the bone, driving through the cortex until loss of resistance.
Remove stylet, confirm placement, secure and connect to extension tubing.

blocks.title: Confirm placement before infusing
blocks.html: A needle that doesn't stand firmly on its own, or a flush that causes visible swelling, means stop and reassess — extravasation into a closed compartment is the complication that turns a good access decision into a bad outcome.

• Extravasation from failure to fully penetrate the cortex or from a through-and-through insertion — monitor the limb for swelling during infusion
  • Compartment syndrome from unrecognized extravasation
  • Fracture, especially in pediatric or osteoporotic bone with excessive force
  • Infection/osteomyelitis with prolonged dwell time — convert to standard IV access as soon as feasible
  • Pain on infusion in conscious patients — pre-treat with intraosseous lidocaine before fluids/medications

IO access is not inferior to IV for emergency medication and fluid administration — treat it as a full-status line, not a placeholder.

The proximal humerus site allows faster flow rates than tibial sites and is preferred when rapid volume resuscitation is the goal.

Always confirm placement before infusing — a needle that doesn't stand firmly on its own, or flush that causes visible swelling, means reassess before continuing.

Convert to standard IV/central access as soon as the situation allows; IO is a bridge, not a destination line.

procedures.title: Junctional Tourniquet Application
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Hemorrhage Control
procedures.subtitle: Hemorrhage control at the junctional zones — groin, axilla, pelvis — where a standard limb tourniquet has no purchase.
procedures.description: Hemorrhage control at groin, axilla, pelvis.

blocks.html:
• Severe, life-threatening hemorrhage at a junctional zone (proximal groin/inguinal, axilla, or pelvic/perineal region) not amenable to standard extremity tourniquet placement
  • Traumatic amputation or penetrating injury at the proximal thigh, groin, or axilla with uncontrolled bleeding

• None absolute in life-threatening junctional hemorrhage
  • Isolated distal extremity hemorrhage where a standard limb tourniquet is more appropriate and simpler to apply

• Commercial junctional tourniquet device (e.g., a pelvic/groin-specific compression device per your agency's stocked device)
  • Wound packing material and hemostatic gauze as an adjunct or backup

steps.html: Expose the injury and identify the junctional zone requiring compression.

Position the device per its specific design — most junctional tourniquets use a target compression pad positioned directly over the vessel proximal to the injury, secured by a belt/strap system anchored around the pelvis or trunk.

Apply and tighten per the device's mechanism (pneumatic, mechanical windlass, or ratchet, depending on the specific device) until bleeding is controlled or a strong distal pulse is lost, whichever the device is designed to target.
Reassess for ongoing hemorrhage; if bleeding continues, adjust positioning or add direct wound packing as an adjunct.

Document application time clearly — junctional tourniquets, like limb tourniquets, carry ischemic risk with prolonged application and should be addressed at the earliest safe opportunity by a receiving surgical team.

blocks.title: Know your specific device before you need it
blocks.html: Junctional tourniquets vary significantly in mechanism between manufacturers, unlike the relatively standardized limb tourniquet — unfamiliarity in the moment costs the time the device exists to save.

• Device-specific misapplication — each junctional tourniquet has a distinct mechanism; unfamiliarity in the moment costs critical time
  • Incomplete hemorrhage control if compression is not directed precisely over the bleeding vessel's proximal course
  • Ischemic injury to the compressed region with prolonged application time
  • Difficulty applying in an uncooperative or actively hemorrhaging, combative patient — may require additional hands

Know your specific issued device's mechanism before you need it — junctional tourniquets vary significantly between manufacturers, unlike the relatively standardized limb tourniquet.

Wound packing with hemostatic gauze remains a critical adjunct or backup when a junctional tourniquet isn't available or isn't fully controlling hemorrhage.

Document time of application prominently on the patient (write it on the device or the patient directly) so the receiving team can immediately assess dwell time.

procedures.title: Lateral Canthotomy
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Cardiac / Neuro
procedures.subtitle: Emergent decompression of orbital compartment syndrome — a vision-saving procedure with a narrow therapeutic window.
procedures.description: Vision-saving orbital compartment decompression.

blocks.html:
• Orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar hemorrhage or rapidly expanding orbital process, typically presenting with proptosis, decreased visual acuity, elevated intraocular pressure, and an afferent pupillary defect
  • Clinical diagnosis with a time-critical window — permanent vision loss can occur within approximately 90-120 minutes of sustained elevated intraocular pressure

• None absolute given the time-critical, vision-threatening nature of true orbital compartment syndrome
  • Globe rupture — canthotomy technique should be adapted with caution, avoiding any additional pressure on the globe itself; some sources still support proceeding if compartment syndrome is confirmed, but extra care is warranted

• Local anesthetic with epinephrine
  • Straight (Mayo/suture) scissors
  • Toothed forceps
  • Hemostat (for the crush technique on the lateral canthal tendon prior to cutting, optional but reduces bleeding)

steps.html: Confirm the clinical diagnosis: elevated intraocular pressure, proptosis, decreased vision, in the setting of trauma or rapid orbital swelling.
Infiltrate local anesthetic with epinephrine at the lateral canthus.
Using a hemostat, crush the lateral canthal tendon area for several seconds to reduce bleeding (optional step, improves hemostasis).
Using straight scissors, perform a lateral canthotomy — a horizontal incision through the lateral canthus, extending from the lateral commissure toward the orbital rim.
Identify the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon by palpating/pulling the lower lid laterally with forceps.
Cut the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon (cantholysis) — this is the step that actually releases the compartment pressure; the canthotomy incision alone is often insufficient.
Reassess intraocular pressure and visual function after cantholysis; if inadequate improvement, consider releasing the superior crus as well.
Arrange urgent ophthalmology follow-up/consultation regardless of immediate improvement.

blocks.title: The canthotomy incision alone is not the therapeutic step
blocks.html: Cutting the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon (cantholysis) is what actually relieves compartment pressure — stopping after the skin incision is a common technical error that leaves the orbit undecompressed.

• Performing the canthotomy incision alone without cantholysis — this is a common technical error and does not adequately decompress the orbit
  • Bleeding at the incision site
  • Inadequate pressure relief requiring release of the superior crus as well
  • Delayed recognition/intervention — the biggest driver of permanent vision loss is time, not technical difficulty of the procedure itself

The canthotomy is not the therapeutic step — the cantholysis (cutting the inferior crus of the tendon) is what actually relieves the compartment pressure. Don't stop after the skin incision.

This procedure is time-critical in a way few others in this library are — roughly a 90-120 minute window before vision loss becomes permanent, so recognition speed matters as much as technique.

Reassess after the inferior crus release; if pressure and proptosis haven't adequately improved, proceed to the superior crus without hesitation.

procedures.title: Massive Transfusion Protocol Activation & Sequencing
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Hemorrhage Control
procedures.subtitle: Getting blood products moving before the lab catches up — ratio-based transfusion as a bridge to definitive hemorrhage control.
procedures.description: Ratio-based transfusion sequencing and logistics.

blocks.html:
• Anticipated or ongoing massive hemorrhage (commonly defined as anticipated need for ≥10 units PRBCs in 24 hours, or ≥4 units in 1 hour, or hemorrhage with hemodynamic instability unresponsive to initial resuscitation)
  • Clinical gestalt of significant ongoing hemorrhage should trigger activation without waiting to meet a strict numeric threshold — the protocol exists to be activated early

• None absolute when major hemorrhage is present or strongly anticipated
  • Known and documented patient refusal of blood products (relative — follow your institution's policy and the patient's expressed wishes/advance directives)

• Institutional MTP activation mechanism (phone activation, EHR order set, or dedicated MTP phone line to blood bank)
  • Rapid infuser/blood warmer
  • Large-bore IV or central access sufficient for high-flow product administration
  • Point-of-care testing (ABG, TEG/ROTEM if available) to guide ongoing product ratios beyond the initial fixed-ratio phase

steps.html: Activate the protocol early and verbally, using your institution's specific activation phrase/mechanism — do not wait for confirmatory lab values in an obviously hemorrhaging patient.
Initiate transfusion in a fixed ratio, typically 1:1:1 (PRBC:FFP:platelets), as the default starting sequence while definitive hemorrhage control is pursued.
Ensure blood is warmed via a rapid infuser/blood warmer system before or during administration to avoid iatrogenic hypothermia.
Administer calcium supplementation proactively — citrate in transfused blood products chelates calcium and can cause clinically significant hypocalcemia during massive transfusion.
Send serial labs (ABG with ionized calcium, fibrinogen, coagulation studies) to guide product ratio adjustments as the resuscitation progresses beyond the initial empiric phase.
Communicate continuously with blood bank regarding ongoing need, product availability, and any anticipated de-escalation.
Formally deactivate the protocol once hemorrhage is controlled and the patient is stabilizing, to avoid unnecessary product waste and cost.

blocks.title: Activate on clinical suspicion, not lab confirmation
blocks.html: The entire value of the protocol is removing decision friction at exactly the moment friction is most costly — waiting for confirmatory labs in an obviously hemorrhaging patient defeats the purpose of having a protocol at all.

• Hypothermia from unwarmed product administration, which independently worsens coagulopathy — part of the lethal triad alongside acidosis and coagulopathy
  • Hypocalcemia from citrate load if calcium is not proactively repleted
  • Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) or transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO), particularly with large product volumes
  • Delayed activation — waiting for lab confirmation before activating costs time the patient may not have
  • Under-transfusion of platelets/plasma relative to PRBCs if ratio discipline is not maintained under the chaos of an active resuscitation

Activate on clinical suspicion, not lab confirmation — the entire value of a protocol is that it removes decision friction in exactly the moment friction is most costly.

Warm the blood and replete calcium proactively rather than reactively — both are easy to forget in the chaos of an active resuscitation and both meaningfully affect coagulation.

The fixed 1:1:1 ratio is a starting point, not a permanent prescription — use point-of-care coagulation data to individualize as soon as it's available.

Deactivate promptly once hemorrhage is controlled; this closes the loop with blood bank and avoids unnecessary product utilization.

procedures.title: Pelvic Binder Placement
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Hemorrhage Control
procedures.subtitle: Circumferential stabilization at the level of the greater trochanters — closing volume in an unstable pelvic ring fracture before hemorrhage becomes uncontrollable.
procedures.description: Circumferential stabilization at the greater trochanters.

blocks.html:
• Suspected unstable pelvic fracture in a trauma patient, especially with hemodynamic instability or a mechanism concerning for pelvic ring disruption
  • Clinical signs: pelvic instability on gentle exam (perform only once, avoid repeated manipulation), leg length discrepancy, rotational deformity, perineal/scrotal hematoma
  • Should be applied empirically in any hemodynamically unstable blunt trauma patient with a concerning mechanism, even before imaging confirmation

• None absolute in suspected unstable pelvic fracture with hemorrhagic shock
  • Confirmed pelvic fracture pattern where binder placement would worsen displacement (rare, and generally not distinguishable in the prehospital/initial resuscitation setting — default to binding when in doubt)
• Commercial pelvic binder device (preferred) or improvised binding (folded sheet)

steps.html: Position the binder at the level of the greater trochanters (not the iliac crests) — this is the correct anatomic level to close the pelvic ring, and the most common placement error is positioning too high.
Apply gentle internal rotation to the lower extremities if feasible before securing, which can help reduce certain fracture patterns.
Wrap the binder circumferentially and secure per the device's mechanism (typically a self-tightening strap/buckle system), applying firm, even circumferential compression.
Avoid over-tightening, which can cause skin injury or, rarely, worsen certain fracture patterns — snug and even compression is the goal, not maximal force.
Reassess distal pulses and skin integrity at the point of pressure after application.
Do not remove or loosen the binder until definitive orthopedic evaluation, even for repeat imaging, unless specifically directed by the trauma/orthopedic team.

blocks.title: Level matters more than almost anything else here
blocks.html: The correct placement is at the greater trochanters, not the belt line — positioning too high is the single most common application error and fails to close the pelvic ring effectively.

• Incorrect placement level (too high, at the iliac crests) failing to achieve effective pelvic ring closure
  • Skin breakdown or pressure injury with prolonged dwell time, particularly over bony prominences
  • Over-tightening causing local tissue injury
  • Repeated pelvic manipulation to "check" stability after binder placement, which can dislodge clot and worsen hemorrhage — assess pelvic stability once, then bind and stop manipulating

Level matters more than almost anything else in this procedure — greater trochanters, not the belt line.

If pelvic fracture is even a reasonable concern in an unstable blunt trauma patient, bind empirically rather than waiting for imaging confirmation.

Once bound, stop examining the pelvis repeatedly — each manipulation risks dislodging early clot formation.

procedures.title: Resuscitative Endovascular Balloon Occlusion of the Aorta (REBOA)
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Vascular Access / Circulatory
procedures.subtitle: Zone selection, balloon inflation, and the discipline of treating occlusion time as a hard clock. A bridge to hemorrhage control, not a treatment in itself.
procedures.description: Zone 1/3 aortic occlusion for non-compressible torso hemorrhage.

blocks.html:
• Non-compressible torso hemorrhage (pelvic, junctional, abdominal) with hemorrhagic shock refractory to initial resuscitation
  • Bridge to definitive hemorrhage control (OR, IR) in a patient too unstable to survive transport or induction without proximal aortic control
  • Peri-arrest or profound hypotension (SBP <70–80 mmHg) from suspected sub-diaphragmatic hemorrhage
  • Alternative to resuscitative thoracotomy in patients with a viable but rapidly deteriorating hemodynamic profile

blocks.title: Survival benefit is not established — this is a bridge, not a proven mortality intervention
blocks.html: The 2023 UK-REBOA trial (Jansen et al., JAMA) randomized exsanguinating trauma patients to standard care with or without REBOA and found no survival benefit from adding REBOA, with a numerically higher mortality in the REBOA arm. Earlier support for REBOA came almost entirely from registry data (AAST AORTA) and non-randomized comparisons, which carry real selection bias — sicker/faster-dying patients are less likely to reach REBOA at all, flattering its apparent outcomes. None of this means REBOA has no role: it still reliably raises proximal blood pressure as a temporizing bridge, and most guidance restricts it to centers with dedicated training, rapid access, and a clear path to definitive control — not as a default first move for non-compressible hemorrhage. Treat it as a technique with a real physiologic effect and an unresolved outcome benefit, not a settled standard of care.

• Known or suspected thoracic aortic injury or dissection proximal to the zone of occlusion
  • Cardiac arrest from a non-hemorrhagic cause — REBOA does not substitute for compressions/defibrillation
  • Inability to obtain femoral arterial access (severe bilateral lower-extremity vascular injury)
  • Prolonged anticipated occlusion time without a clear path to definitive control (irreversible ischemia risk beyond ~30–60 min at Zone 1)

• REBOA catheter kit (7 Fr low-profile system where available, or 11–12 Fr standard system)
  • Ultrasound with linear probe for femoral access
  • Arterial sheath, guidewire, compliant occlusion balloon
  • Pressure monitoring line/transducer (proximal, and distal if possible)
  • Fluoroscopy or external landmark measurement for balloon positioning if fluoro unavailable
  • Saline for balloon inflation — never air

steps.html: Obtain common femoral artery access via ultrasound-guided Seldinger technique; confirm arterial waveform.
Place introducer sheath appropriate to catheter system.
Determine target zone: Zone 1 (left subclavian to celiac trunk) for suspected intra-abdominal hemorrhage; Zone 3 (lowest renal artery to aortic bifurcation) for isolated pelvic hemorrhage.
Measure catheter insertion length externally (xiphoid for Zone 1, umbilicus for Zone 3) or confirm with fluoroscopy if available.
Advance catheter to target zone.
Inflate balloon slowly with saline while monitoring proximal pressure rise and loss of distal pulse/waveform — stop inflation at the minimum volume achieving occlusion.
Confirm occlusion: rising proximal MAP, loss of distal femoral signal.
Document inflation time immediately; set a hard countdown for the team.
Proceed to definitive hemorrhage control (OR/IR) without delay — REBOA is a bridge, not a treatment.
Deflate gradually in a controlled setting, titrating to hemodynamics — rapid deflation risks reperfusion collapse.

blocks.title: Occlusion time is the whole safety margin
blocks.html: Zone 1 REBOA carries a real ischemia-reperfusion burden that climbs with dwell time — treat balloon inflation time as a hard countdown communicated out loud to the team, not a detail to check later.

• Ischemia-reperfusion injury distal to occlusion, worsening with time — minimize occlusion duration
  • Distal limb ischemia/thromboembolism from sheath or catheter
  • Balloon rupture or malposition — confirm zone before inflation
  • Rebound hypotension on deflation — deflate incrementally with volume/pressor support ready
  • Missed proximal (thoracic) injury — occluding downstream of an undiagnosed thoracic injury will not control hemorrhage and delays recognition
  • Vessel injury/dissection from access or catheter advancement

Zone selection matters more than perfect technique — get the level right before worrying about elegance.

Treat occlusion time like a ticking clock out loud to the team; nobody should be surprised at minute 30.

REBOA buys time, it doesn't fix anything — the moment it's inflated, the next question is where definitive control is happening and how fast.

If ultrasound-guided access is failing under time pressure, don't burn the clock — escalate to cutdown or your backup access plan early.

procedures.title: Wound Packing with Hemostatic Agents
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Hemorrhage Control
procedures.subtitle: Direct pressure taken to its logical extreme — packing the wound cavity itself, not just covering the surface.
procedures.description: Direct pressure taken into the wound cavity itself.

blocks.html:
• Hemorrhage from a wound not amenable to tourniquet application (junctional zones, torso, neck) or where a tourniquet is not yet in place/not fully effective
  • Deep or cavitating wounds where surface pressure alone fails to control bleeding

• None absolute for life-threatening hemorrhage
  • Superficial wounds with easily controlled bleeding by direct pressure alone (packing is unnecessary escalation)

• Hemostatic gauze (e.g., agents impregnated with a topical hemostatic compound) preferred over plain gauze when available
  • Standard gauze as an acceptable substitute if hemostatic gauze is unavailable
  • Gloved hands for direct packing

steps.html: Expose the wound fully; clear visible pooled blood/clot to identify the actual bleeding source if possible.
Pack the gauze directly into the wound cavity, in continuous contact with the bleeding source, using firm and deliberate pressure as you pack — this is not a light fill, it's a firm, dense pack.
Continue packing until the entire cavity is filled and no dead space remains.
Apply firm, sustained direct manual pressure over the packed wound for a minimum of 3 minutes (or per your hemostatic agent's specific instructions) without releasing to check.
After the sustained pressure period, apply a pressure dressing over the packed wound to maintain compression.
Reassess for continued bleeding through or around the dressing; if hemorrhage continues, repack or escalate (additional packing, tourniquet if anatomically feasible, or surgical control).

blocks.title: Sustained pressure means sustained
blocks.html: The 3-minute hold before checking is not optional — releasing pressure early to check the wound is the most common reason a correctly packed wound still appears to keep bleeding.

• Inadequate packing density leaving dead space where bleeding continues unseen beneath the dressing
  • Releasing pressure too early to "check" the wound, interrupting clot formation
  • Retained packing material if not clearly documented and communicated to the receiving team
  • Incomplete hemorrhage control in wounds with a bleeding source not reachable by packing alone (requires surgical or endovascular control)

Pack it like you mean it — a light or loose pack that leaves dead space is functionally no better than no packing at all.

The 3-minute sustained pressure interval is not optional; resist the urge to check the wound before that time has passed.

Hemostatic gauze improves outcomes over plain gauze, but plain gauze packed correctly and held under sustained pressure is still far better than no packing.

Clearly document what was packed and where — retained packing material needs to be tracked and removed appropriately downstream.
